Guided trip

Black holes

Three real black holes: where they are and how we know. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Black holes

A black hole you can point to

This is the Swan, flying along the Milky Way. In its neck is Cygnus X-1, the first thing in the sky that astronomers agreed was a black hole. You cannot see it. Nobody can. It was found in 1964, because it is one of the strongest sources of X-rays in the sky.

What a black hole is

Seven thousand light-years from home. A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that nothing gets out, not even light. This one has about twenty times the mass of the Sun. The mark in the middle is ours. The scatter of dots to one side is home: the stars this map has measured.

The centre of the galaxy, from home

Look past the spout of the Teapot, where the Milky Way is brightest. Twenty-seven thousand light-years that way is the centre of our galaxy. In the middle of it sits a black hole four million times as massive as the Sun.

Sagittarius A star

Nobody can see this black hole itself. Astronomers watched a star go round it every sixteen years, at millions of kilometres an hour, and worked out what it circles. Eight radio observatories, working as one telescope the size of the Earth, then photographed glowing gas and a shadow. Here it is drawn as a model, from its mass.

The first picture of a black hole

Far beyond our galaxy, in the galaxy M87, is a black hole with the mass of six and a half billion Suns. In 2019 eight radio telescopes working together made the first picture of one. Here it is drawn as a model. Its dark shadow is bigger than our whole Solar System.

Nothing to fear

The Sun will never be a black hole: only stars many times heavier end that way. And if you swapped the Sun for a black hole of the same mass, the planets would stay in their orbits. It would only get a lot colder. The nearest black hole we know is about fifteen hundred light-years away.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, OpenNGC and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
